n: That same day, the king gives Haman’s estate to Esther. She reveals that Mordecai is her cousin and guardian, and he is brought before the king.

f.g: His property and household; Persian kings confiscated the estates of traitors.

n: The king gives Mordecai the signet ring he took from Haman — making Mordecai the new chief minister. Esther puts him in charge of Haman’s estate. The reversal is complete.
But the danger is not over: the decree to kill the Jews still stands. Esther again risks approaching the king, falling at his feet in tears, pleading for her people.
Once more the king extends the golden scepter, and Esther rises to speak.
With great tact, she asks that Haman’s letters be overturned. She blames Haman, not the king, wisely allowing the king to save face.

f.w: reverse the letters devised by Haman
f.g: She calls them Haman’s letters, though they were sealed in the king’s name.

n: Her heartfelt plea: how could I bear to watch my people and family be destroyed? Esther’s concern is now fully for others, not herself.
The king reminds them of what he has already done: given Haman’s house to Esther and executed Haman.

f.w: he laid his hand upon the Jews
f.g: He plotted to attack the Jews.

n: Since a royal decree cannot be reversed, the king authorizes them to write a new decree in his name as they see fit. They cannot cancel the first law, but they can counter it.
The new decree is written about two months after Haman’s, in every language — including, this time, Hebrew for the Jews themselves.

f.w: to the Jews according to their writing
f.g: Unlike Haman’s decree, this one was also sent to the Jews in their own script.

n: Mordecai seals it with the king’s ring and sends it out with the fastest couriers — on horses and royal mules bred for speed.

f.g: Probably swift horses or mules bred from the royal stables; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: The decree allows the Jews to gather and defend themselves against anyone who attacks them — using the same words as Haman’s decree, now turned in their favor.

f.w: to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish

n: Their right to self-defense applies on the very same day set for their destruction: the thirteenth of Adar.

f.w: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month

n: This decree is also posted publicly, so everyone knows the Jews can now fight back.

f.w: to avenge themselves on their enemies
f.g: To defend themselves and repay those who attack them.

n: The couriers race out on the king’s urgent order.
Mordecai leaves the palace dressed in royal blue, white, and purple, with a golden crown. The city that had been confused by Haman’s decree now celebrates.
For the Jews, darkness turns to light, mourning to gladness and honor. A short, poetic verse of pure relief.

f.g: A Hebrew image for joy, deliverance, and life.

n: Everywhere the decree arrives, Jews feast and celebrate. Many non-Jews even join themselves to the Jewish people, sensing that their God was with them.

f.w: many of the people of the land became Jews
f.g: Some converted; others may have simply identified with the Jews for safety.
